title: AF after ischemic stroke: anticoagulation timing
summary: Start the DOAC early once AF-associated ischemic stroke is confirmed and hemorrhage excluded. CATALYST (5,441 patients from 4 trials): starting within 4 days vs day 5 or later reduced 30-day recurrent ischemic stroke, sICH or unclassified stroke (2.1 vs 3.0%; OR 0.70), with identical sICH (0.4%). ELAN schedule: within 48 h for minor or moderate and day 6–7 for major imaging-defined infarcts. OPTIMAS: within 4 days was noninferior to days 7–14 (3.3% each).

recommendations.text: In carefully selected (e.g., milder severity) AIS patients with atrial fibrillation, a strategy of early oral anticoagulation post-stroke is low risk and is reasonable compared with delayed anticoagulation, although the efficacy of early anticoagulation for preventing early recurrent stroke is not established.

In stroke or TIA patients with AF who do not have moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve, a DOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, or rivaroxaban) is recommended over warfarin to reduce recurrent stroke risk.

consider: Size the infarct on imaging (ELAN categories), not by NIHSS alone; brain imaging before starting may be considered (AHA 2021, 2b).

ELAN infarct size: minor ≤1.5 cm; moderate involves a cortical superficial branch of the MCA, ACA or PCA, a deep MCA branch or the internal border zone; major involves an entire MCA, ACA or PCA territory, two or more MCA cortical branches, cortical plus deep MCA branches, or a brainstem or cerebellar lesion >1.5 cm (ELAN, NEJM 2023).
Hemorrhagic transformation: starting or continuing anticoagulation may be considered case by case (AHA 2026, 2b).
TIA with AF: anticoagulate immediately (AHA 2021, 2a); use a DOAC over warfarin unless there is a mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis.
caution: Trial schedules guide but do not set an individual start date for very large infarcts or significant hemorrhagic transformation.

title: Stroke mechanism, ESUS and rhythm monitoring
summary: Define the mechanism before choosing prevention, with testing started within 48 h: brain CT or MRI, ECG, and CBC, coagulation, glucose, HbA1c, creatinine and lipids (AHA 2021, COR 1), plus carotid and intracranial vessel imaging. Cryptogenic stroke: echocardiography and prolonged rhythm monitoring are reasonable (2a) — CRYSTAL AF found AF in 12.4 vs 2.0% at 12 months with an implantable monitor. ESUS: antiplatelet, not empiric anticoagulation — NAVIGATE ESUS (rivaroxaban), RE-SPECT ESUS (dabigatran) and ARCADIA (apixaban for atrial cardiopathy) were neutral.
consider: Classify the mechanism (TOAST); an incomplete workup leaves it undetermined and does not establish ESUS.
ESUS: TEE, cardiac CT or cardiac MRI might be reasonable to find cardioaortic sources (2b).
Who reviews the monitor and acts on AF?
caution: A brief negative ECG does not exclude paroxysmal AF.

title: TOAST classification and stroke mechanism
summary: TOAST sorts ischemic stroke into five subtypes: large-artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, small-vessel occlusion, other determined etiology and undetermined etiology, each labeled possible or probable by the clinician's certainty; interrater agreement was high. Assign the subtype after brain imaging, vessel imaging and cardiac evaluation, because the mechanism decides prevention (antiplatelet or anticoagulant, revascularization, PFO closure).
consider: An incomplete workup leaves the mechanism undetermined; it does not establish ESUS.
DWI pattern helps: a single deep lacune suggests small-vessel disease, scattered emboli in several territories a cardiac source, and a watershed pattern large-artery disease (AHA TIA statement).
Lateral medullary infarction (n=130): vertebral artery disease in 67% and PICA disease in 10%; mechanisms were large-vessel 50%, dissection 15%, small-vessel 13% and cardioembolic 5%.
caution: TOAST was built to classify trial participants; it does not replace an individual mechanism review.

title: PFO: attribution and closure discussion
summary: PFO closure is reasonable for ages 18–60 with nonlacunar stroke of undetermined cause after a full evaluation and a PFO with high-risk features (AHA 2021, 2a); without high-risk features the benefit is uncertain (2b). RESPECT: recurrent ischemic stroke 0.58 vs 1.07 per 100 patient-years (HR 0.55) over a median 5.9 years; CLOSE: 0/238 vs 14/235 strokes over a mean 5.3 years. Closure adds AF (CLOSE 4.6 vs 0.9%) and venous thromboembolism (RESPECT).
consider: Exclude competing causes first: vessel imaging, prolonged rhythm monitoring and echocardiography with a bubble study.
Use RoPE and PASCAL to judge whether the PFO is likely causal.
Discuss procedural risk, AF and the long-term antiplatelet plan with the closure team.
caution: Evidence over age 60 and for an incidental PFO is limited.

title: Carotid stenosis: symptoms, severity and referral
summary: Symptomatic 70–99% stenosis: endarterectomy if perioperative stroke or death risk is <6% (AHA 2021, COR 1); 50–69%: endarterectomy depending on patient factors (COR 1); <50%: no revascularization (COR 3). Operate within 2 weeks of a nondisabling event (2a); at age ≥70 or within the first week, endarterectomy is preferred over stenting (2a). Asymptomatic ≥70%: CREST-2 found fewer 4-year events with stenting plus intensive medical management (2.8 vs 6.0%) but no significant benefit from endarterectomy (3.7 vs 5.3%); ACST-2 found stenting and endarterectomy similar (5-year non-procedural stroke 5.3 vs 4.5%).

recommendations.text: CEA is recommended for patients with TIA or nondisabling ischemic stroke within the past 6 months and ipsilateral severe (70-99%) carotid stenosis to reduce future stroke risk, provided the estimated perioperative morbidity and mortality is below 6%.

When carotid revascularization is indicated for TIA or nondisabling stroke, it is reasonable to perform the procedure within 2 weeks of the index event rather than delaying surgery, to increase the likelihood of a stroke-free outcome.

consider: How was the stenosis measured (NASCET), and does the lesion explain the event?
Large or disabling infarct, hemorrhage or near-occlusion: individualize timing with vascular surgery.
Everyone gets intensive medical therapy: antiplatelet, statin and BP control (COR 1).
caution: CREST-2 ran two separate trials, so it does not compare stenting directly with endarterectomy.

title: Symptomatic intracranial atherosclerosis
summary: Severe (70–99%) symptomatic intracranial stenosis within 30 days: aspirin plus clopidogrel for up to 90 days (AHA 2021, 2a; AAN 2022), high-intensity statin with LDL <70 mg/dL, long-term SBP <140 and exercise (COR 1). No angioplasty or stenting as first treatment (COR 3: Harm) — SAMMPRIS: 30-day stroke or death 14.7 vs 5.8% with stenting. BASIS (China) tested submaximal balloon angioplasty in selected patients; it does not establish routine intervention.
consider: Confirm the stenosis is symptomatic and in the right territory; 50–69% stenosis gets medical therapy (stenting is harmful).
Write the DAPT stop date and the single agent to continue.
Recurrent events despite therapy: recheck adherence and mechanism; the usefulness of angioplasty or stenting is unknown (2b).
caution: Long-term BP targets do not apply in the acute, perfusion-dependent phase.

title: Cervical artery dissection
summary: Give antithrombotic therapy for at least 3 months (AHA 2021, COR 1); aspirin or anticoagulation are both reasonable (AHA 2026, 2a). CADISS found no difference (stroke or death 3/126 vs 1/124); TREAT-CAD did not show aspirin noninferior to a vitamin K antagonist (composite 23 vs 15%; 7 ischemic strokes vs none). Reassess the regimen with symptoms and follow-up imaging.

recommendations.text: In AIS patients with extracranial carotid or vertebral arterial dissection, treatment with either antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for at least 3 months is reasonable to prevent recurrent stroke.

consider: Confirm on CTA or MRI/MRA and separate cervical from intracranial or aortic dissection.
Recurrent events despite antithrombotics: endovascular therapy may be considered (AHA 2021, 2b).
Look for an underlying arteriopathy such as FMD when the history suggests it.
caution: Neither trial was powered to prove equivalence, and DOACs were not tested.

title: Secondary prevention and medication review
summary: Noncardioembolic stroke: antiplatelet rather than anticoagulant (COR 1); DAPT only short term (minor stroke/TIA 21–30 days; severe intracranial stenosis up to 90 days). BP <130/80 for most (AHA 2021, COR 1). Atherosclerotic stroke: statin ± ezetimibe to LDL <70 mg/dL (COR 1; Treat Stroke to Target events 8.5 vs 10.9%); no known coronary disease and LDL >100: atorvastatin 80 mg (SPARCL). Recheck lipids 4–12 weeks after a change, then every 3–12 months.

recommendations.text: Antiplatelet therapy is recommended over oral anticoagulation for patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or TIA to reduce recurrent ischemic stroke and other cardiovascular events while minimizing bleeding risk.
An office BP goal of less than 130/80 mmHg is recommended for most hypertensive stroke or TIA patients to reduce recurrent stroke and vascular events.

For ischemic stroke or TIA patients with atherosclerotic disease (intracranial, carotid, aortic, or coronary), lipid-lowering therapy with a statin (plus ezetimibe if needed) to achieve an LDL-C goal below 70 mg/dL is recommended to reduce major cardiovascular events.

consider: Is the mechanism settled, and does it change the drug (AF, PFO, dissection, intracranial stenosis)?
Very high risk with LDL >70 despite statin plus ezetimibe: a PCSK9 inhibitor is reasonable (2a).
Check adherence, cost, smoking, diet and activity at every visit.
caution: Avoid indefinite DAPT or antiplatelet-plus-anticoagulant combinations without a separate indication.

title: Recovery, rehabilitation and follow-up
summary: Start formal interdisciplinary rehabilitation assessment in hospital (AHA 2026, COR 1) and avoid high-dose mobilization within 24 h (COR 3: Harm). Screen for depression with a structured inventory and treat it (COR 1); SSRIs do not improve motor recovery (COR 3). Reassess function, mood and goals at follow-up and re-engage therapy when needs change.
consider: Which impairments, daily activities and participation goals need assessment or renewed therapy?
Have the patient and care partner received education, training and support?
Is follow-up feasible (transport, access, telehealth), and who reassesses progress?
caution: A screening score is not a diagnosis, and this card gives no driving, work or travel clearance.
